chapter: Chapter 3: The Rise of the Marathas

leaders.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
leaders.summary: Born in the Bhonsle clan to Shahji and Jijabai; envisioned Swarajya, pioneered guerrilla warfare, founded the Maratha Navy (1657), escaped Agra (1666), and was crowned at Raigad (1674).
leaders.chsFact: Title: 'Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati'; started Rajyabhisheka shaka; instituted Ashta Pradhan Mandala; forbade Dutch slave trade.

leaders.name: Rajmata Jijabai
leaders.summary: Raised young Shivaji in the Pune jagir while Shahji served in the Deccan, instilling strong moral values, education, and the dream of self-rule.
leaders.chsFact: Supervised Shivaji's upbringing and early administration in Pune.

leaders.name: Shahji Bhonsle
leaders.role: Father of Shivaji & Deccan Military Chief
leaders.summary: A prominent Maratha noble in the Bhonsle clan who served the Deccan sultanates and held the Pune jagir.
leaders.chsFact: Shivaji's Sanskrit royal seal proudly names him 'the son of Shahji'.

leaders.name: Chhatrapati Sambhaji
leaders.summary: Escaped Agra with Shivaji in 1666 and later became the sole obstacle to Aurangzeb's Deccan conquest after Bijapur and Golconda fell.
leaders.chsFact: Brutally tortured and executed by Aurangzeb; his sacrifice galvanised decades of Maratha resistance.

leaders.name: Chhatrapati Rajaram
leaders.summary: Became Chhatrapati after Sambhaji's execution and shifted the Maratha base to Gingee (Tamil Nadu), keeping the Mughal army stretched across South India.
leaders.chsFact: Successfully preserved Maratha sovereignty from Gingee Fort.

leaders.name: Maharani Tarabai
leaders.summary: Wife of Rajaram who led the empire after his death. Realising North India was unprotected while Aurangzeb was tied down in the Deccan, she sent armies northward.
leaders.chsFact: Known as the 'architect of the northward Maratha expansion'.

leaders.name: Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj
leaders.summary: Presided over the Maratha state during its pan-Indian rise alongside Peshwa Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa.
leaders.chsFact: NCERT Fig. 3.20 displays his handwriting in the cursive Modi script.

leaders.name: Ahilyabai Holkar
leaders.summary: Governed central India wisely after losing her husband and son, building temples, ghats, wells, and roads from Kedarnath to Rameswaram.
leaders.chsFact: Rebuilt Kashi Vishwanath (Varanasi) & Somnath (Gujarat); revitalised Maheshwar weaving industry (MP).

leaders.name: Peshwa Bajirao I
leaders.summary: Instrumental in transforming the Maratha kingdom into a rapid pan-Indian power across central and northern India.
leaders.chsFact: 'Peshwa' is a Persian term meaning Prime Minister (Marathi: Pantapradhan).

leaders.name: Nanasaheb Peshwa
leaders.summary: Expanded Maratha influence to its widest territorial reach, bringing Delhi (1754) and briefly Lahore, Attock, and Peshawar under Maratha sway.
leaders.chsFact: Shown in counsel with Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj in NCERT Fig. 3.10.

leaders.name: Peshwa Madhavrao I
leaders.role: Peshwa Who Rebuilt Power After Panipat
leaders.summary: Restored Maratha strength, prestige, and northern influence remarkably quickly after the 1761 defeat at Panipat.
leaders.chsFact: Oversaw the Maratha resurgence that culminated in recapturing Delhi in 1771.

leaders.name: Mahadji Shinde (Scindia)
leaders.summary: Recaptured Delhi in 1771 and built a large, disciplined European-style army with modern artillery.
leaders.chsFact: Kept Delhi under Maratha control for three decades; key victor in the First Anglo-Maratha War.

leaders.name: Nana Phadnavis
leaders.summary: Organised the first pan-Indian anti-British alliance, uniting even old rivals like Hyder Ali of Mysore and the Nizam of Hyderabad.
leaders.chsFact: Depicts British surrender before Nana Phadnavis & Mahadji Shinde (NCERT Fig. 3.11).

leaders.name: Kanhoji Angre
leaders.summary: Guided the Maratha Navy to numerous victories over European ships using coastal geography and clever tactics.
leaders.chsFact: Challenged European cartaz (naval passes) and demanded passes from Europeans, who called him a 'pirate'.

leaders.name: Ramachandrapant Amatya
leaders.summary: Served as Shivaji's Finance Minister (Amatya) and authored the royal treatise Adnyapatra ('The Royal Edict') on statecraft.
leaders.chsFact: Warned against European 'hat-wearers' and wrote that 'Forts are the core of the state'.

leaders.name: Sant Dnyaneshwar
leaders.summary: Brought the philosophy of the Bhagavad Gita and Upanishads into Marathi, making spiritual wisdom accessible to ordinary people.
leaders.chsFact: Helped lay the deep cultural foundation of Maharashtra.

leaders.name: Sant Namdev
leaders.summary: Composed devotional songs in the language of the masses, promoting equality and devotion across regions.
leaders.chsFact: His teachings united diverse communities beyond rigid ritualism.

leaders.name: Sant Tukaram
leaders.summary: Composed devotional abhangas (poetry) in simple Marathi that deeply shaped Maharashtra's spiritual and social consciousness.
leaders.chsFact: Featured on an Indian commemorative postal stamp (NCERT Fig. 3.4).

leaders.name: Sant Ramdas
leaders.summary: Combined spiritual devotion with social organisation and political awareness (similar to the Sikh Gurus), inspiring strength and self-reliance.
leaders.chsFact: Featured in NCERT Fig. 3.3 as a key pillar of Maharashtra's cultural awakening.

leaders.name: Poet Bhushan
leaders.summary: Travelled specifically to Maharashtra to meet Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and composed celebrated heroic poetry in his praise.
leaders.chsFact: Shows Shivaji's pan-Indian fame during his own lifetime.

leaders.name: Maharaja Chhatrasal
leaders.summary: So inspired by Chhatrapati Shivaji's struggle against Mughal rule that he established an independent kingdom in Bundelkhand (UP & MP).
leaders.chsFact: Direct example of Shivaji's Swarajya ideal spreading to North India.

leaders.name: Ekoji (Venkoji)
leaders.summary: Half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji who conquered Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu), starting a flourishing southern Maratha dynasty.
leaders.chsFact: Marked the start of Tamil-Telugu-Marathi syncretic culture in Thanjavur.

leaders.name: Raja Serfoji II
leaders.summary: Multilingual scholar who wrote Devendra Kuravanji, patronised Carnatic music & Bharatanatyam, founded Dhanwantari Mahal, and set up India's first native printing press.
leaders.chsFact: Inscribed Bhonsle history in Marathi on the Brihadishwara temple wall.

leaders.name: Afzal Khan
leaders.summary: Sent by the Bijapur Sultanate to crush Shivaji; met Shivaji one-on-one at Pratapgad Fort where Shivaji defeated him in close combat.
leaders.chsFact: Defeated using the wagh nakh (tiger's claw) followed by guerrilla ambush.

leaders.name: Shaista Khan
leaders.summary: Invaded Maratha territory for three years before Shivaji raided his camp at night like a surgical strike.
leaders.chsFact: Barely escaped, lost a few fingers, and promptly left Maharashtra.

leaders.name: Mirza Raja Jai Singh & Aurangzeb
leaders.summary: Jai Singh defeated Shivaji at Purandar Fort (1665) and persuaded him to visit Agra; Aurangzeb imprisoned Shivaji (1666) and later spent decades fighting the Marathas in the Deccan.
leaders.chsFact: Aurangzeb died in the Deccan (1707) without ever subduing the Marathas.
